117 F.3d at 587—88. At first glance, it may seem that Paralyzed Veterans 
simply notes the absence of a red flag identified in American Mining 
Congress (i.e., even without the manual, DO J would not lack a legal basis 
for enforcement) and concludes that the rule is interpretive. But the 
opinion does more: it suggests that a rule is more likely to be interpretive, 
and therefore exempt from notice and comment, if its content (1) is “fairly 
encompassed within” the preexisting statute or legislative rule that it 
purports to construe, (2) is “tightly * * * drawn linguistically from the 
actual language of the [preexisting] statute or rule,” or (3) is not “distinct 
or additive to the [preexisting] regulation” or statute. Id. at 588. On the 
prevalence of this kind of test for identifying interpretive rules in the D.C. 
Circuit and elsewhere, see Ronald M. Levin, Rulemaking and the Guidance 
Exemption, 70 Ad min . L. Re v . 263, 324^335 (2018).
What is the D.C. Circuit trying to do in Paralyzed Veterans and its 
progeny? The opinion appears to be saying that the making of some rules 
involves the exercise of power and policy choice whereas the making of 
’
others—^rules whose content is already largely determined by some other 
j
preexisting statute or rule—does not. Notice and comment is necessary for 
the former (policy-choosing) variety of rulemaking, but unnecessary for the 
latter (ministerial) variety. This distinction would seem difficult to draw in 
a predictable way.
For an inventive attempt to operationalize the principle at which 
Paralyzed Veterans aims, consider Hoctor v. USDA, 82 F.3d 165 (7th Cir. 
1996). In implementing the Animal Welfare Act, the United States 
Department of Agriculture (USDA) promulgated a notice-and-comment 
rule, under the heading “structural strength,” which stated that a facility 
containing an animal “must be constructed of such material and of such 
strength as appropriate for the animals involved. The * * * facihties shall 
be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the 
animals from injury and to contain the animals.” 9 C.F.R. § 3.125(a). USDA 
then issued a memorandum stating that section 3.125(a) required an eight- 
foot-high fence for the enclosure of lions, tigers, and other big cats. The 
agency cited Hoctor, a dealer in such animals, for keeping big cats within 
a fence lower than the memorandum’s required eight feet. Hoctor argued 
that the memorandum was a legislative rule, while the agency said it was 
interpretive. The Seventh Circuit, per Judge Posner, sided with Hoctor:
